pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; determine the unknown whole number in a × or ÷ equation relating three numbers (8×?=48, ?×6=42, ?÷5=9).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 'solve missing number problems' involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.4 — 'determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers, e.g. 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ? ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?'.
• Operational details — this applies division-as-unknown-factor and the ×÷ inverse to solve for a missing value in ANY position (missing factor, missing product, missing dividend/divisor/quotient). The key strategy is rewriting via the fact family: 8×?=48 → 48÷8=?; ?÷5=9 → ?=9×5. Children must attend to WHERE the unknown sits, because the rescue operation differs (a missing dividend is found by multiplying, a missing factor by dividing). This also nurtures the relational (not operational) view of '=' as balance, seeding algebra. Use the bar model and fact-family triangle; cover one number and decide how to find it.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): find a missing factor with a known fact (7×?=63). Tier B (age 8–9): find the unknown in any position, including ?÷5=9 (missing dividend). Tier C (age 9): explain the strategy for each position and check by substituting back.
bestPractices: Use the fact-family triangle: cover any one of the three numbers and decide whether to × or ÷ to find it — making the unknown's position drive the method.
Rewrite the equation using the inverse (8×?=48 → ?=48÷8; ?÷5=9 → ?=9×5) and verbalise why.
Stress the relational meaning of '=' as balance, not 'the answer comes next', to prevent left-to-right misreading and seed algebra.
Include unknowns in every position (factor, product, dividend, divisor, quotient), not just missing products.
Always check by substituting the found value back into the original equation.
keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle — cover-a-number to choose the operation
Bar model — whole/part structure showing which quantity is missing
Balance/scale image — the relational equals sign
commonMisconceptions: Applying the same operation regardless of the unknown's position (e.g. always dividing), so a missing dividend is wrong.
Reading '=' operationally ('do something to get the answer') rather than as balance, mishandling 5 = ?÷3.
Treating division as commutative when rewriting (?÷5=9 → ?=5÷9).
Guess-and-check without using the inverse, which is slow and error-prone.
Not checking the answer back in the original equation.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year-olds: find the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three numbers, with the unknown in ANY position (missing factor 8×?=48 or ?×6=42, missing product 6×7=?, missing dividend ?÷5=9, missing divisor 48÷?=6, missing quotient 42÷6=?). The central idea is that the operation you use to 'rescue' the unknown depends on WHERE the gap sits: a missing factor is found by dividing, a missing dividend by multiplying. Build this on the fact-family/inverse relationship and a relational (balance) reading of '=', and always check by substituting the found value back into the original equation.

activities.title: Cover-and-solve with a fact-family triangle
feedback: If a learner always divides regardless of position, point to the covered corner on the triangle: when the TOP (product/dividend) is hidden, the two bottom numbers are multiplied to find it.
When a learner correctly flips the operation as the gap moves, name it: 'You chose the operation from where the gap was — that's the whole strategy.'
If a learner treats ?÷5=9 as 5÷9 or 9÷5, show that division is not commutative here: ?÷5=9 rearranges to ?=9×5=45, and checking 45÷5=9 confirms it.
activities.rationale: Making the unknown's position drive the method, and seeing one trio solve several equations, is intended to build the position-dependent strategy rather than a single memorised move. The fact-family/inverse structure supports missing-number reasoning.
sourceClaims: The fact-family/inverse strategy and a relational (balance) meaning of '=' support missing-number work and seed algebra.
Y3–Y4 pupils solve missing-number problems involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
3.OA.4 requires determining the unknown in a × or ÷ equation relating three whole numbers, in any position.
learnerActions: Work with one trio of linked numbers, e.g. 6, 7 and 42 arranged on a fact-family triangle (42 at the top as the product; 6 and 7 at the bottom as the factors).
Cover one of the three numbers and decide: to find THIS number, do I multiply or divide? State your choice aloud before revealing.
Now cover a DIFFERENT number of the same trio and decide again. Notice when the operation flips: cover 42 (acting as product or dividend) → multiply 6×7; cover a factor like 7 → divide 42÷6.
Write the matching equation for each covered case: 6×?=42, ?×6=42, 42÷?=6, and ?÷6=7. Confirm the single trio solves them all.
Say in your own words: 'What I do — times or divide — is decided by WHERE the gap is, not by the numbers.'
If a bar model or balance view is available, use it to see which quantity (whole or part) is missing and recolour/update it as you solve.
activities.intendedInsight: The operation needed to find an unknown is determined by its position in the equation (missing factor → divide; missing dividend/product → multiply), and one fact family generates every related missing-number equation.

activities.title: Rewrite with the inverse, then check by substituting back
feedback: If a learner subtracts or adds the two visible numbers (e.g. treats 7×?=63 as 63−7=56), restate it as 'seven times WHAT is 63?' and reach for the times-table fact or 63÷7.
If a learner reaches the right method but makes a fact slip, don't reteach the strategy — have them check by substituting back, which surfaces the arithmetic error.
Praise substituting-back as the habit that catches mistakes: 'Putting it back in and seeing it balance is how you know you're right.'
activities.rationale: Explicit inverse-rewriting and a balance meaning of '=' are intended to help counter left-to-right misreading and reduce the division-commutativity error, and the substitute-back habit is intended to seed algebraic checking.
sourceClaims: The fact-family/inverse strategy and a relational (balance) meaning of '=' support missing-number work and seed algebra.
Y3–Y4 pupils solve missing-number problems involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
learnerActions: Take a missing-number equation and rewrite it using the inverse operation, saying why: 8×?=48 becomes ?=48÷8; ?÷5=9 becomes ?=9×5.
Solve the rewritten equation using a known fact rather than guessing.
Substitute your answer back into the ORIGINAL equation and check both sides are equal, e.g. for ?=45: 45÷5=9 ✓.
Try the relational reading of '=' with a reversed equation like 5=?÷3: read '=' as 'both sides balance', find ?=15, and check 5=15÷3.
Compare rewriting-with-the-inverse to trial-and-error on 7×?=63: find it directly with 63÷7=9 and notice the inverse avoids repeated guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: Rewriting an equation with the inverse operation gives the unknown directly, and substituting back verifies it; '=' means both sides balance, not 'the answer comes next'.

activities.title: Mixed-position practice and spot-the-error
feedback: If a learner divides when a missing dividend needs multiplying (producing e.g. 1.8 from 9÷5), return to the fact-family triangle: with 5 and 9 at the bottom, the missing dividend sits at the top and is found by multiplying, 9×5=45.
For the reversed equation 5=?÷3, if the learner stalls, remind them '=' balances both sides; ?÷3 must equal 5, so ?=15.
Reinforce the discriminating point: a single fixed move (always divide, or always multiply the two shown numbers) will fail at least one item — the position tells you which operation.
activities.rationale: Deliberately varying the unknown's position and including error-analysis targets the most common misconceptions and is intended to check that the strategy generalises rather than being tied to one format.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.4 requires determining the unknown in a × or ÷ equation relating three whole numbers, in any position.
Y3–Y4 pupils solve missing-number problems involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
learnerActions: Solve a set with the unknown in every position: 8×?=48 (missing factor), ?×6=42 (missing factor), ?÷5=9 (missing dividend), 48÷?=6 (missing divisor), 42÷6=? (missing quotient), 6×7=? (missing product), 5=?÷3 (reversed).
For each, first say which operation you need and WHY, then solve.
Spot-the-error: review a worked solution where ?÷5=9 was 'solved' as ?=5÷9, explain what went wrong, and give the correct value with a check.
Answer: 'Which operation finds a missing dividend — multiply or divide?' and justify with an example.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency comes from correctly choosing the operation by position across all cases, and from recognising common wrong moves (fixed operation, treating division as commutative).

activities.title: Talk it through: 'what's missing, times or divide?'
feedback: If explanations default to 'I just divided', press for the position reason: 'Which number was hidden, and why does that mean divide?'
Encourage checking each stated fact-family member against the trio so none is missed or malformed.
activities.rationale: A Socratic exchange can rehearse the reasoning and the relational view, complementing hands-on work; it is a useful rehearsal of justification rather than a substitute for manipulating cases. Spoken justification does not by itself guarantee the strategy transfers to independent written work.
sourceClaims: The fact-family/inverse strategy and a relational (balance) meaning of '=' support missing-number work and seed algebra.
learnerActions: With a partner or adult, play a 'mystery number' game: one person hides a value in an equation, the other must say how they'll find it (which operation and why) before computing.
Explain the strategy for each position in words: why a missing factor is found by dividing and a missing dividend by multiplying.
Write out the full fact family for a trio you are given, e.g. 7, 9 and 63: 7×9=63, 9×7=63, 63÷7=9, 63÷9=7.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the choice of operation and generating the full fact family externalises the reasoning and is intended to help consolidate relational understanding.

constraints: Include unknowns in EVERY position (factor, product, dividend, divisor, quotient), not just missing products.
Always require checking by substituting the found value back into the original equation.
Emphasise the relational meaning of '=' (both sides balance), not 'the answer comes next', to prevent misreading reversed equations like 5=?÷3.
Division is not commutative: ?÷5=9 rearranges to ?=9×5, never 5÷9 or 9÷5. Correct this error directly rather than leaving it uncorrected.

A fill-in-the-blank or multiple-choice format is well suited to assessing across positions but, being fixed, tests the strategy more than it elicits the position-dependent reasoning; pair it with manipulable or verbalised work for teaching.
A static tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a clean strategy anchor but does not let the learner try many cases with feedback; use it alongside active practice.

Optional supports such as a bar model, a balance view, live recolouring of the missing quantity, or a hidden-card triangle make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording has been qualified accordingly.
Self-audit arithmetic check: 8×6=48, 7×9=63, 63÷7=9, 9×5=45 and 45÷5=9, 6×7=42, 48÷6=8, 15÷3=5 all verified correct as used.
The legacy claim that '3D adds cost without insight' for this topic has been removed as an unsupported universal; the comparative efficacy of representations is not established by the cited sources.
Two of three sources are marked verified:false in the original row (CCSS-M 3.OA.4 and NCETM guidance); the standards content is widely known but was not re-checked here.

The error pattern 'child divides when missing dividend needs multiplication, giving 1.8' (9÷5=1.8) is retained ONLY as a diagnostic signal; the activity corrects it to ?=9×5=45 and never presents 1.8 as an acceptable answer.

The 'Talk it through' activity cites the fact-family/relational source for the content being rehearsed; that source does not establish that a conversational format is effective or necessary, so the medium's benefit is stated only as a narrow affordance.

probeDeeper: How did you find what goes in the box for 7 × □ = 63?
For □ ÷ 5 = 9, why do you multiply rather than divide?
How can you check your box value is right by putting it back in?
Write the fact family that goes with 7, 9 and 63.
assess.correctAnswer: 9 (7×9 = 63, or 63÷7); 45 (because □÷5 = 9 means □ = 9×5). The teacher watches for the child using the inverse operation / related fact — recognising the first as a missing-factor and the second as a missing-dividend recovered by multiplying.

errorPatterns.pattern: operates on the two visible numbers with the operation shown — for □ ÷ 5 = 9 computes 9 ÷ 5 or 5 ÷ 9 rather than 9 × 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the fact-family triangle: with 5 and 9 at the corners the missing dividend is at the top, found by multiplying; the ÷ sentence rearranges to ×.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides when the missing dividend needs multiplication, giving 1.8 or similar

errorPatterns.pattern: adds/subtracts to fill the box — treats 7 × □ = 63 as 63 − 7 = 56
errorPatterns.nextMove: restate as 'seven times WHAT is 63' and reach for the times-table fact or 63÷7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child subtracts or adds the two numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: relies on slow trial-and-error, plugging numbers in, with no use of known facts or inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: show the inverse gives the answer directly (63÷7 = 9); trial-and-error is unnecessary once the relationship is seen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child tries 7×5, 7×6… until it works, rather than dividing

errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child check by substituting the answer back into the equation.

responseLevels.gap: adds/subtracts to fill boxes, or divides when the missing dividend needs multiplication; no inverse reasoning.
responseLevels.full: uses the inverse relationship / related fact to find the unknown in any position, explains the strategy, and checks by substituting back.
responseLevels.partial: solves the missing-factor case via a known fact but mishandles the missing-dividend case, or leans on trial-and-error.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to find the missing number in each while you watch their method: 7 × □ = 63, then □ ÷ 5 = 9. Encourage them to say how they worked it out. Watch whether they use a related multiplication/division fact and the inverse relationship, or resort to trial-and-error.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two boxes sit in different positions (missing factor vs missing dividend), and children who apply one fixed move (always divide, or always multiply the two visible numbers) fail one. Watching the method reveals whether they reason from the inverse relationship or guess-and-check.
